definition: The pudendum, or pudenda, (S, O, Msb, K,) of a human being, (S, O,) of a man and of a woman: (TA:) so called because it is abominable to uncover, and to look at, what is thus termed: (Msb:) said in...
sourceDefinition: The pudendum, or pudenda, (S, O, Msb, K,) of a human being, (S, O,) of a man and of a woman: (TA:) so called because it is abominable to uncover, and to look at, what is thus termed: (Msb:) said in the B to be from EaArN , meaning ma*am~apN : (TA:) [but see what is said voce EaAriy~apN : the part, or parts, of the person, which it is indecent to expose: ] in a man, what is between the navel and the knee: and so in a woman: (Jel in xxiv. 31:) or, in a free woman, all the person, except the face and the hands as far as the wrists; and respecting the hollow of the sole of the foot, there is a difference of opinion: in a female slave, like as in a man; and what appears of her in service, as the head and the neck and the fore arm, are not included in the term Ewrp . (TA.) [ AlEaworapu Almugal~aZapu means The anterior and posterior pudenda: AlEaworapu Almuxaf~afapu , the other parts included in the term Ewrp : so in the law-books.] The covering what is thus termed, in prayer and on other occasions, is obligatory: but respecting the covering the same in a private place, opinions differ. (TA.) definition: (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K) and sometimes EaAriyapN , without teshdeed, (Msb, K,) when used in poetry, (Msb,) and ↓ EaArapN , (S, O, K,) What is taken by persons by turns;
sourceDefinition: (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K) and sometimes EaAriyapN , without teshdeed, (Msb, K,) when used in poetry, (Msb,) and ↓ EaArapN , (S, O, K,) What is taken by persons by turns; expl. by maA tadaAwaluwhu bayonahumo : (K:) [generally meaning a loan: and the act of lending; ] the putting one in possession of the use of a thing without anything given in exchange: (KT, and Kull p. 262:) the returning of the thing thus termed is obligatory, when the thing itself remains in existence; and if it has perished, then one must be responsible for its value, accord. to Esh-Sháfi'ee, but not accord. to Aboo-Haneefeh: (TA:) pl. [of the first] EawaAriY~u , (S, O, Msb, K,) and [of the second] EawaArK . (Msb, K.) A poet says, waA@loEawaAriY~u qaSaArN A^ano turado A_in~amaA A^anofusunaA EaAriy~apN [ Our souls are only a loan: and the end of loans is their being given back: turado being for turad~a ]. (S, O.) EaAriy~apN is of the measure faEoliy~apN : Az says that it is a rel. n. from EaArapN , which is a subst. from A_iEaArapN : (Mgh, * Msb:) Lth says that what is thus called is so called because it is a disgrace ( EAr ) to him who demands it; and J says the like; and some say that it is from EaAra Alfarasu , meaning, “ the horse went away from his master: ” but both these assertions are erroneous; since EAry~p belongs to art. Ewr , for the Arabs say humo yataEaAwaruwna AlEawaAriY~a , meaning they lend [ loans ], one to another; and EaArN and EaAra Alfarasu belong to art. Eyr : therefore the correct assertion is that of Az. (Msb.)

definition: Anything that causes disease in the eye, (K, TA,) and wounds: so called because the eye becomes closed on account of it, and the person cannot see, the eye being as it were blinded: (TA:) ophthalmia;
sourceDefinition: Anything that causes disease in the eye, (K, TA,) and wounds: so called because the eye becomes closed on account of it, and the person cannot see, the eye being as it were blinded: (TA:) ophthalmia; syn. ramadN ; (S, O, K;) as also ↓ Euw~aArN : (Msb:) which latter also signifies foul, thick, white matter, that collects in the inner corner of the eye; not fluid; syn. ramaSN : (Msb:) or both signify a fluid matter that makes the eye smart, as though a mote, or the like, had fallen into it: (Lth:) and both signify a mote, or the like, (S, O, K,) in the eye: (S:) or (TA, in the K “ and ”) EaAy^irN signifies pimples, or small pustules, in the lower eyelid: (K:) a subst., not an inf. n., nor an act. part. n.: (TA:) the pl. of ↓ Euw~aArN is EawaAwiyru , and, by poetic license, EawaAwiru . (TA.) One says ↓ biEayonihi Euw~aArN , meaning, In his eye is a mote, or the like. (S.) ― -b2- EayonN EaAy^irapN An eye in which is the fluid matter called ↓ Euw~aAr : but when the eye has this, you do not say of it EaArato . (Lth.) ― -b3- EaAy^iru AlEayoni (assumed tropical:) What fills, or satisfies, the eye ( maA yamolaw^uhaA ), of maAl [meaning camels or the like], so as almost to put it out; and in like manner EaAy^irapu Eayonayoni . (TA.) One says, Einodahu mina AlmaAli EaAy^irapu EayonK , (S, O,) or EaAy^irapu Eayonayoni and ↓ Eay~irapu Eayonayoni , (K, but with Ealayohi in the place of Einodahu , and in the CK Eitorapu is put for Eay~irapu ,) both of these mentioned by Lh, (TA,) i. e. (assumed tropical:) [ He has, of camels or the like ], what fill, or satisfy, ( tamolaA^u ,) his sight by the multitude thereof; (K;) or that at which the sight is confounded, or perplexed, by reason of the multitude thereof, as though it filled, or satisfied, the eye, and put it out: (S, O:) [and A'Obeyd says the like:] or, accord. to As, the Arab in the Time of Ignorance used, when his camels amounted to a thousand, to put out an eye of one of them; and hence, by EaAy^irapu AlEayoni they meant a thousand camels, whereof one had an eye put out. (TA.) -A2- EaAy^irN also signifies An arrow of which the shooter is not known; (S, O, K;) and in like manner, a stone: (S, O:) pl. EawaAy^iru : (TA:) EawaAy^iru nabolK means arrows in a scattered state, of which one knows not whence they have come. (IB, TA.) [See also art. Eyr .] And EawaAy^iru (S, O, K) and ↓ EiyraAnN (K) signify Swarms of locusts in a scattered state: (S, O, K: [or] the first thereof going away in a scattered state, and few in number. (TA.)

definition: Blind of one eye: (K:) one-eyed;
sourceDefinition: Blind of one eye: (K:) one-eyed; wanting one eye: or having one of his eyes sunk in its socket: (Msb:) or having one of his eyes dried up: (IKtt:) applied to a man, (S, Msb,) and to a camel, &c.: (TA:) fem. EaworaA='u : (Msb:) pl. EuwrN and EuwraAnN (O, K) and EiyraAnN . (K.) The A^aEowar is considered by the Arabs as of evil omen. (TA.) It is said in a prov., A^aEowaru Eayonaka waAlHajara [ O oneeyed, preserve thine eye (thine only eye) from the stone ]. (Meyd, TA.) ― -b2- Squint-eyed; syn. A^aHowalu : (TA:) and EaworaA='u the same, applied to a woman. (K, TA.) ― -b3- A crow: (S, O, K:) so called as being deemed inauspicious; (S, O, TA;) or by antiphrasis, (TA,) because of the sharpness of his sight; (S, O, TA;) or because, when he desires to croak, he closes his eyes; (O, TA;) and ↓ EuwayorN is the dim., (S, O,) and signifies the same. definition: She (a woman, S) let down, or let fall, her [ head-covering called ] qnAE upon her face.
sourceDefinition: She (a woman, S) let down, or let fall, her [ head-covering called ] qnAE upon her face. (S, K.) 'Antarah says, A_ino tugodifiY duwniY AlqinaAEa faA_in~aniY Tab~N biA^axo*i AlfaArisi Almusotaloy^imi (S,) i. e. If, O my beloved, thou let down before me the head-covering, meaning if thou veil thyself from me, I am expert in capturing the mail-clad horseman: then how should I lack power to capture thee? (EM p. 236.) ― -b2- [Hence,] Agdf All~ayolu (tropical:) The night let down its curtains [ of darkness ]. (S, K.) ― -b3- And Al$~abakapa EalaY AlS~ayodi He (a sportsman, or fowler, or the like,) let fall the net upon the object, or objects, to be captured. (S, K.) Hence, (TA,) it is said in a trad., A_in~a qaloba Almuw^omini A^a$ad~u A@rotikaADFA mina Al*~anobi yuSiybuhu mina AlEuSofuwri Hiyna yugodafu bihi (S, TA,) i. e. [ Verily the heart of the believer is more vehemently agitated in consequence of the offence that he purposes than the sparrow ] when the net is made to cover it, whereupon it struggles to escape: (TA:) or mina AlxaTiyoy^api [i. e. in consequence of the sin that he is tempted to commit]. (So in the O, instead of min Al*nb ySybh .) ― -b4- Agdf bihaA (assumed tropical:) He compressed her, (Ibn- 'Abbád, O, K,) i. e., a woman: (Ibn-'Abbád, O:) or, as in the A, he went in to her. (TA.) ― -b5- Agdf said of the sea [app. from the same verb said of the night] (tropical:) It became confusedly agitated in its waves; expl. by the words AiEotakarato A^amowaAjuhu . (TA.) ― -b6- And (assumed tropical:) He slept. (AA, TA in art. sdf .) ― -b7- And, accord. to Lh, (O,) Agdf said of the circumciser (O, K, TA) of a boy (O) means He cut off entirely the prepuce; (O, K, TA;) like A^asoHata ; (O, TA;) but ISd holds that the latter has this meaning, and the former means he left somewhat thereof: (TA:) one says to the circumciser, laA tugodifo walaA tusoHito , (O, TA,) but this means Leave not thou much of the skin, nor cut off entirely. (TA.)

definition: , aor. , (S, K,) inf. n. garaDN , (S, A, K,) He was vexed, or disquieted by grief, and by distress of mind; he was grieved, and distressed in mind: he was disgusted; he turned away with disgust. (S,...
sourceDefinition: , aor. , (S, K,) inf. n. garaDN , (S, A, K,) He was vexed, or disquieted by grief, and by distress of mind; he was grieved, and distressed in mind: he was disgusted; he turned away with disgust. (S, A, K.) You say, gariDa minohu He was vexed by, or at, him, or it, and disquieted by grief, and by distress of mind; he was grieved, and distressed in mind, by him, or it: (Mgh in art. grD , and TA:) he was disgusted with it, or at it; he turned away from it with disgust: (Mgh:) and he feared him, or it. (Ibn-'Abbád, K, TK: but the first and second mention only the inf. n. of the verb in this last sense.) And gariDa biAlmuqaAmi , aor. and inf. n. as above, [ He was vexed, &c., by continuance, stay, residence, or abode, in a place: he was disgusted with it, or at it. ] (S.) And A_i*aA faAtahu AlgaraDu fat~ahu AlgaraDu i. e. AlD~ajaru [ When the object of aim, or endeavour, escapes him, so that he cannot attain it, vexation, or disquietude by grief, and by distress of mind, or disgust, crushes him ]. (A, TA.) ― -b2- And hence, (A,) aor. as above, (K,) and so the inf. n., (A, TA,) He yearned, or longed: (S, A, K:) or he yearned, or longed, vehemently, or intensely: (TA:) A_ilayohi for him, or it: (S:) or A_ilaY liqaAy^ihi for meeting with him: the verb in this sense being made trans. by means of AlY because it imports the meaning of Ai$otaAqa and Han~a [which are made trans. by the same means]: (A, TA:) [for] accord. to Akh, gariDotu A_ilayohi signifies gariDotu mino h`w^ulA='i A_ilayohi [ I turned with vexation, or disgust, from these, to him, or it ]; because the Arabs connect the verb [with its objective complement] by means of all these particles [mentioned above; namely, b and mn and AlY ]. definition: A butt, a mark, or an object of aim, at which one shoots, or throws;
sourceDefinition: A butt, a mark, or an object of aim, at which one shoots, or throws; (S, O, Msb, K;) a thing that thou settest up ( maA A^amovalotahu ) to shoot or throw at: (IDrd:) pl. A^agoraADN . (Msb, K.) It is said in a trad., laA tat~axi*uwA $ayoy^FA fiyhi Alr~awHu garaDFA [ Ye shall not take a thing in which is the vital principle as a butt ]. (TA.) And hence one says, Aln~aAsu A^agoraADu Almaniy~api (assumed tropical:) [ Mea are the butts of destiny, or of death ]: and jaEalotaniY garaDFA li$atomika (assumed tropical:) [ Thou madest me, or hast made me, a butt for thy reviling ]. (TA.) ― -b2- And hence, (tropical:) An object of aim or endeavour or pursuit, of desire or wish, or of intention or purpose: (Msb:) a scope; or any end which one endeavours, or seeks, or intends, or purposes, to attain: (B:) an object of want, and of desire: (TA:) the advantage, or good, which one seeks, or endeavours, or purposes, to attain, or obtain, from a thing: so much used in this tropical sense as to be, in this sense, conventionally regarded as proper. (MF.) You say, garaDuhu ka*aA (tropical:) His object of aim or endeavour or pursuit, &c., is such a thing: (Msb:) or his object of want, and of desire, is such a thing (TA.) And faEala ligaraDK SaHiyHK (tropical:) He did, or acted, for a just, or right, object of aim &c. (Msb.) And fahimotu garaDaka (assumed tropical:) I understood, or have understood, thine object of aim &c., or thine intention; syn. qaSodaka . (S.) [See another ex. voce gariDa , of which it is also the inf. n.]

definition: , (S, O, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, O, K,) aor. , (K,) inf. n. gaDofN , (TA,) He broke it, namely, a branch, or stick, or the like, (S, O, K, TA,) and a thing, (TA,) but not thoroughly. (S, O, TA.) [See also 2.] ― -b2- And gaDafa A^u*unaha , (S, O, K,) aor. and inf. n. as above, (S, O,) He (a dog) relaxed his ear, and folded, or creased, it: (S, O, K, TA:) [see, again, 2:] or gaDafa A^u*unaha , inf. n. gaDofaAnN and gaDafaAnN , he (a dog) twisted his ear: and in like manner one says of the wind, [ gaDafatohaA ,] i. e. it twisted it. (TA.) And gDaf AlwisaAdapa He folded the pillow [ so as to make creases in it ]. (Ham p. 785. [But perhaps this is correctly ↓ gD~f : comp. its quasi-pass., 5.]) ― -b3- gaDafato said of [wild] she-asses, (O,) or of a she-ass, (K,) aor. as above, (O, TA,) and so the inf. n., (TA,) signifies A^axa*ati AljaroYa A^axo*FA [as though meaning They, or she, restrained the running, i. e. their, or her, running; agreeably with what here follows]: (O, K, TA:) gaDafa , [for gaDafa mina AljaroYi ,] said of a horse &c., means he lessened, lit. took from, the rate of the running, ( A^axa*a mina AljaroYi ,) without reckoning: (L, TA:) Umeiyeh Ibn-Abee- 'Áïdh El-Hudhalee says, yaguD~u wayagoDifona mino ray~iqK (O, TA) meaning He (the ass) withholds somewhat of his running, ( yakuf~u baEoDa jaroyihi ,) and they (the she-asses) lessen, lit. take from, the [or rather a ] first, or former, rate of their running, ( yaA^oxu*ona A^axo*FA mino A^aw~ali jaroyihin~a ,) without reckoning: (Skr: see Kosegarten's “ Carmina Hudsailitarum, ” p. 189:) Skr says, in explanation of the citation above from Umeiyeh, that gaDofN signifies the act of taking and lading out [with the hand] ( A^axo*N and garofN ); and on one occasion he says, the taking easily; [adding,] one says, gaDafa fulaAnN mino TaEaAmK lay~inK [ Such a one took, or laded out with his hand, from soft food ]. (TA.) -A2- gaDafa AlEayo$u , inf. n. guDuwfN , The life was soft, or easy, and plentiful. (TA.) -A3- gaDifa , [aor. , inf. n. gaDafN ,] He (a dog, S) was, or became, relaxed, or flabby, in the ear. (S, K, TA.) And gaDifati AlA^u*unu , inf. n. gaDafN , is said to mean The ear was, or became, long and relaxed or flabby: or it advanced upon the face: or it retired towards the head: or its extremities folded upon the inner part thereof: or, in a dog, it turned towards the back of the neck: or it became folded, or creased, naturally. (TA.) [See also gaDafN , below: and see 7.] ― -b2- gaDifa All~ayolu : see 4.

sourceDefinition: [inf. n. of gaDifa (q. v.): and, as a simple subst.,] Laxness, or flabbiness, in the ear: (S, O, K:) or, as in the T, a laxness, or flabbiness, of the upper part [ of each ] of the two ears, upon, or over, the concha thereof, by reason of its width and its largeness: (TA:) Aboo-'Amr Esh-Sheybánee says, after citing a verse of Abu-n-Nejm, describing a lion, that it signifies a twisting, in the ear, backwards: accord. to ISh, it is, in the lion, a laxness, or pendulousness, of the upper eyelids, upon the eyes; arising from anger and pride: (O:) and he says that, accord. to some, it is, in the lion, abundance of the fur, and a folding, or creasing, of the skin. (TA.) And one says, [app. in relation to the lion,] ↓ fiY A^a$ofaArihi gaDofN and gaDafN [app. In the edges of his upper eyelids is a laxness, or pendulousness ]; both meaning the same. (TA.) ― -b2- Also Softness, or easiness, and plentifulness, of life: (S:) like gaTafN . (O in art. gTf .) -A2- And A species of tree in India, exactly like the palm-tree, (Lth, O, K,) except that (K) its fruit-stones are divested of covering, without a liHaA=' [or pulpy pericarp ], and from its lowest to its uppermost part it has green saEaf [or branches like those of the palm-tree ], (Lth, O, K,) covered [ thereby ]: (Lth, O:) AHn says, it is a plant resembling the palm-tree exactly, (O, L, TA,) but not growing tall, (TA,) having many saEaf , and prickles, and [ leaves such as are termed ] xuwS , of the hardest sort, whereof are made large [ receptacles of the kind called ] jilaAl [pl. of jul~apN ], that serve for sacks, goods being carried in them by land and by sea; (O, L, TA;) it produces from its head unripe dates of disagreeable flavour, not eaten; and, he says, of its xuwS are made mats like carpets, (L, TA,) called simaAm , pl. of sum~apN [q. v.], (L,) one of which may be spread for twenty years. (L, TA.) -A3- See also the next paragraph, in two places.

sourceDefinition: , applied to a dog, Relaxed, or flabby, in the ear; pl. guDofN ; (S, O, K;) occurring in a verse of Dhu-r-Rummeh, cited voce Ea*abN ; (O, TA;) and the fem. gaDofaA='u is applied [to a bitch, and] to an ear: (TA:) or a dog having the upper part of his ear folded, or creased, backwards; and ↓ gaADifN when it is forwards. definition: , (S, O,) or AlA^adiyma , (K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, O,) or AlA^adiyma , (K,) aor. , inf. n. gamolN , He folded the skin, or hide, and buried it, in order that it might become soft, or flaccid, and pliant, when its wool was pulled: (S, O: *) if neglected for a while, it becomes spoiled, or marred: the epithet applied to it is ↓ gamiylN ; (S, O;) and gamiynN also: (S:) or he spoiled, or marred, the skin, or hide: or he put it in the bottom of some receptacle ( fiY gum~apK ), [ and left it a while, ] in order that its wool might become detached: (K:) or he buried it, (K, TA,) having folded it, (TA,) in the sand, (K, TA,) after moistening [ it ], (TA,) in order that it might become stinking, and its hair [or wool ] might be plucked off: (K, TA:) or, accord. to AHn, he folded it while it was moist, and left it folded longer than it required, so that it became spoiled, or marred: or, as some say, he folded it after it was tanned, then covered it a day and a night, so that its hair, or its wool, became loose, when it was plucked off: if left more than a day and a night, it becomes spoiled, or marred: (TA:) and ↓ Agml signifies [the same: (see gaSaba Aljiloda :) or] he left his skin, or hide, [ buried, or put in the bottom of some receptacle, &c., while moist, ] until it became spoiled, or marred. (TA.) ― -b2- And gamala Alt~amora , (S,) or Albusora , (O, K,) He did in like manner to the dates, or the unripe dates, in order that they might become ripe: (S, O, K:) and the epithet applied to them is ↓ magomuwlN ; and magomuwnN . (TA.) ― -b3- And gamala AlEinaba , (K, TA,) aor. and inf. n. as above, (TA,) He put the grapes together, in quantities one above another, (K, TA,) in the basket of palm-leaves. (TA.) ― -b4- gamala fulaAnaA He covered such a one, (K, TA,) with clothes, (TA,) in order that he should sweat. (K, TA.) ― -b5- gamala AljuroHa He put pieces of rag, one above another, upon the wound. (O, TA.) ― -b6- gamala AlA^amora He hid, concealed, or covered, the affair, or case. (TA.) ― -b7- And gamala Al$~ayo'a , (K,) inf. n. gamolN , (O,) He put the thing into a good, sound, right, or proper, state. (O, K.) -A2- gamala Aln~abaAtu , (O, K,) inf. n. gamolN , (TA,) The plants, or herbage, became accumulated, one, or one part, overlying another, (O, K, TA,) so as to become withered, and decayed. (TA.) [See also 5.] -A3- gamila Aln~abotu , the verb being like fariHa , The plant, or plants, or herbage, became in a bad, or corrupt, state. (TA.) ― -b2- And one says gamila h`*aA AlmakaAnu biAln~aboti [app. meaning This place became, or has become, in a bad, or corrupt, state by reason of the herbage: or concealed, or covered, by herbage; as may be inferred from an explanation of A^aroDN gamilapN ]. (O.) ― -b3- And gamila AljuroHu , (TA,) inf. n. gamalN , (K,) The wound became in a bad, or corrupt, state, by reason of the bandage. (K, TA.)

definition: A wide, depressed piece of ground or land, (ISh, S, O, Msb, K,) but not much depressed, and in some instances having acclivities [ bordering it ];
sourceDefinition: A wide, depressed piece of ground or land, (ISh, S, O, Msb, K,) but not much depressed, and in some instances having acclivities [ bordering it ]; (ISh;) sometimes, as they assert, a league ( farosax ) in extent, and having in it meadows; (AHn;) and ↓ gaATN and ↓ gawoTN signify the same; (O, K;) or the last is more depressed than the gAy^T : (IDrd, O:) and gAy^T is also applied to a valley: (TA:) the pl. [of pauc.] is A^agowaATN , (S, Msb, K,) or this is pl. of gawoTN , (IB,) and [of mult.] giyTaAnN , (S, Msb, K,) which is pl. of both these sings., (IB,) and guwTN (S, Msb, K) and giyaATN . (K.) ― -b2- Hence, (tropical:) A place in which one satisfies a want of nature; the custom being to do so in a depressed place, where one is concealed. (S, * Msb, * TA.) In the Kur [iv. 46, or v. 9], accord. to an extraordinary reading, it is written ↓ gayoT , [a form now commonly used, and signifying a garden, but there meaning a privy place, ] the original form of which may be gayowiT , and then gay~iT , [and then gayoT ,] it being contracted; or, accord. to Abu-l- Hasan, the Y may be originally w , these two letters being in this instance interchangeable. (IJ.) You say, A^ataY AlgaAy^iTa , (S, TA,) and Daraba AlgaAy^iTa , (TA,) (tropical:) He satisfied a want of nature; (S, TA;) voided excrement, or ordure. (TA.) ― -b3- And hence, (S, TA,) (tropical:) Human excrement, or ordure: (S, K, TA:) because they used to cast it away in a gAy^T : or because they used to go thither to satisfy a want of nature. (TA.)

(O, TA.)

sourceDefinition: [in my copies of the S written AifotiyaAl ] is of the measure AifotiEaAlN from AlfaA^olu : (S, K, * TA: *) [in the PS and TK, it is said to be syn. with tafaA^~ulN : it seems, however, that in the ex. here following, its exact signification, and whether it be used in an act. or a pass. sense, is doubtful; and that it is trans. without a prep.:] El-Kumeyt says, describing horses, A_i*aA maA bdato taHota AlxawaAfiqi Sad~aqato biA^ayomani faA^oli Alz~aAjiriyna A@fotiy^aAluhoA [app. meaning, When they appear beneath the standards, (perhaps standards set up as winningposts,) the regarding them as of good omen, or their being regarded as of good omen, (by reason of their excellent performance,) verifies the happiest augury of the diviners: with respect to its being made fem. in this ex., though not regularly fem. in form, see SarofN , third sentence]. (O, TA.)

definition: , (T, S, M, O, Msb, K,) and faAlN without ' is allowable, (Msb,) A good omen;
sourceDefinition: , (T, S, M, O, Msb, K,) and faAlN without ' is allowable, (Msb,) A good omen; (PS;) contr. of TiyarapN : (T, M, Msb, K:) it is when a man is sick, and he hears another say yaA saAlimu [O safe]; or seeking, and hears another say yaA waAjidu [O finder]: (ISk, T, S, O, K: *) or it is when one hears a good saying, and augurs good by it: (Msb:) [therefore] it is said in a trad., kaAna yuHib~u AlfaA^ola wayakorahu AlT~iyarapa [ He (the Prophet) used to like the fA^l , and dislike the Tiyarap ]: (T, S, O:) [or it signifies so, and likewise an evil omen: i. e.] it is used in relation to a good saying and to an evil saying, (AZ, T, Msb, K,) by some of the Arabs: (T:) it is said in a trad. [of the Prophet], yuEojibuniY AlfaA^olu AlS~aAliHu [ The good fA^l pleases me ]; which shows that there is a sort of fA^l that is good and a sort that is not good: (TA:) and [in like manner] TaAy^irN is applied to that which is good and that which is evil: (K in art. Tyr :) the pl. is A^afow^ulN [properly a pl. of pauc.], (S, O,) or fuw^uwlN [a pl. of mult.], (M,) or both: (K:) El-Kumeyt says, walaA A^asoA^alu AlT~ayora Eam~aA taquwlu walaA tataxaAlajuniY AlA^afow^ulu [ And I will not ask the birds respecting what they say, nor shall omens, or good omens, contend with me as though pulling me in different directions ]. (S, O.) ― -b2- laA faA^ola Ealayoka means No harm shall befall thee; (T, O, K;) and no evil fortune; and no mischief. (T.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , (T, S, M, O, K,) inf. n. favo'N (T, M, K) and fuvuwo'N , (M, K,) both inf. ns. from Lh, (M,) He stilled, or allayed, the boiling of the pot, (T, S, M, O, K,) with water, (S, O,) i. e. with cold water, or by lading out with the ladle: (T:) and vafaA^ahaA signifies the same. (M.) ― -b2- [Hence] one says, A^aTofaA^a fulaAnN Aln~aAy^irapa wafavaA^a Alquduwra AlfaAy^irapa (tropical:) [ Such a one extinguished the discord, or rancour, or enmity, and stilled the boiling passions ]. (A, TA.) ― -b3- And favaA^a gaDabahu , (M, K, *) aor. , (M, K,) inf. n. favo'N , (M,) (tropical:) He stilled, or quieted, or abated, his anger, (M, K, * TA, *) by words, or otherwise. (TA.) A_in~a Alr~aviyoy^apa tafovaA^u AlgaDaba (assumed tropical:) [ Verily what is termed rvyy^p stills, or appeases, anger ] is one of their provs., (S, O, TA,) expl. in art. rvA^ . (TA.) ― -b4- And favaA^otu Alr~ajula , (S, O,) or favaA^otuhu Ean~iY , (T, TA,) (assumed tropical:) I averted, or turned back, the man from me, by words, or otherwise. (T, S, O, TA.) And favaA^a Al$~aYo'a Eanohu , (M, K,) inf. n. favo'N , (M,) (assumed tropical:) He averted the thing from him. (M, K, TA.) And maA favaA^aka Ean~aA (assumed tropical:) What withheld, or has withheld, thee from us? (Har p. 180.) ― -b5- Also favaA^a Al$~aYo'a , (M, K,) aor. , inf. n. favo'N and fuvuwo'N , (TA,) He allayed the cold of the thing by heating. (M, K, TA.) And favaA^ati Al$~amosu AlmaA='a The sun abated, or allayed, the cold of the water. (M.) And favaA^ahu , inf. n. favo'N , He heated it; namely, water, (AZ, T, O,) &c. (T.) And accord. to MF, the phrase favaA^a All~abana is allowable [as meaning He boiled the milk so that it frothed up and became curdled, or clotted, or dissundered: see what next follows]. (TA.) -A2- favaA^a All~abanu , aor. , The milk was boiled so that it frothed up and became curdled, or clotted, or dissundered: (AHát, M, O, K:) when this is the case, the milk is termed ↓ faAviy^N . (AHát, O.) -A3- faviy^ati Alqidoru The cookingpot ceased to boil. (O.) ― -b2- And faviy^a [or faviy^a gaDabuhu ] (assumed tropical:) His anger was, or became, abated; (TA;) [and] so gaDabuhu ↓ AnfvA^ . (Har p. 232.) ― -b3- And maA tafovaA^u tafoEalu (assumed tropical:) Thou dost not cease doing [such a thing]; like mA tafotaA^u . (A, TA.) -A4- favaA^a bisaloHihi : see faTaA^a .

sourceDefinition: , [aor. ; and app. fariga , aor. and , as below; inf. n. furuwgN and faraAgN ; or, accord. to some, the latter is a simple subst., but it is more commonly used than the former;] said of a thing, It was, or became, empty, vacant, void, devoid, destitute, or unoccupied; syn. xalaA . (Msb.) [You say, faraga mino ka*aA It was, or became, empty, vacant, void, devoid, or destitute, of such a thing; or unoccupied thereby. ] And faraga laka Al$~aYo'u [ The thing was, or became, vacant, or unoccupied, for thee; as though it were a place, or a vessel: and hence, the thing was, or became, exclusively for thee ]. (TA voce xalaA .) ― -b2- [Hence,] faraga (O, * K, * TA) said of a man, (TA,) [and app. fariga also, as below,] inf. n. furuwgN , (tropical:) He died; (O, K, TA;) because his body became devoid of his soul, or spirit. (TA.) ― -b3- And faraga mina Al$~ugoli , (S, O, Msb, K, *) aor. , inf. n. furuwgN (S, O, Msb, K) and [more commonly] faraAgN , (S, O, K,) or the latter is a simple subst.; (Msb;) and farag , aor. , (O, K,) mentioned by Yoo; (O;) and fariga , aor. , (O, Msb, K,) of the dial. of Temeem; (Msb;) and fariga , aor. , a compound of two dial. vars.; (O, Msb;) He was, or became, vacant from, devoid of, or free from, business, occupation, or employment; unoccupied, unemployed, or at leisure. (K, * TA.) [See also 5.] ― -b4- [And hence, faraga mina AlA^amori He ceased from, ended, or finished, the affair. ] ― -b5- And faraga lahu and A_ilayohi , (O, Msb, K, TA,) aor. and ; (TA;) and fariga , (O, * Msb, K, * TA,) aor. ; inf. n. furuwgN and [more commonly] faraAgN ; (TA;) He made him, or it, his object, or the object to which he directed himself; syn. qaSada : (O, Msb, K, TA:) [or he made him, or it, his exclusive object; agreeably with an explanation of the phrase here following]: whence, in the Kur [lv. 31], lakumo sanaforugu We will make you our object; expl. by IAar as meaning sanaEomidu [which is syn. with sanaqoSidu ]; (TA;) and some read sanaforagu ; (O, TA;) and some, saniforagu ; (O;) and some, saniforigu , asserting that Temeem say niEolimu ; (O, TA;) and some, sanaforagu A_ilayokumo , meaning sanaqoSidu A_ilayokumo ; or sanaforugu lakumo means We will apply ourself exclusively ( sanatajar~adu ) to the reckoning with, and the requiting of, you; and it is said to be a threat; (Bd;) a metaphorical phrase, from a man's saying to him whom he threatens, saA^aforugu laka , (Ksh, Bd,) meaning I will apply myself exclusively to the making an assault upon thee: (Ksh:) one says [also] in threatening, laA^aforugan~a laka [meaning in like manner I will assuredly apply myself &c.]. (TA.) [See, again, 5.] ― -b6- fariga AlmaA='u , (S, O, K,) aor. , (S, K,) inf. n. faraAgN , (S, TA,) The water poured out or forth, or became poured out or forth. (TA.) ― -b2- farugati AlD~arobapu (tropical:) The [ wound made by a ] stroke, or blow, was wide; (O, K, TA;) likened to the farog of the leathern bucket. (TA.) ― -b3- And faraAgapN (as an inf. n. of which the verb is faruga , TK) signifies The being impatient, and disquieted or disturbed or agitated. (O, K.) -A3- faraga as trans.: see 4.

definition: I made it empty, vacant, void, devoid, destitute, or unoccupied;
sourceDefinition: I made it empty, vacant, void, devoid, destitute, or unoccupied; as also ↓ A^aforagotuhu . (Msb.) taforiygu AlZ~uruwfi signifies The making the receptacles empty. (S, O, K.) And some read [in the Kur xxxiv. 22], Hat~aY A_i*aA fur~iga Eano quluwbihimo , (O, TA,) expl. as meaning Until, when their hearts shall be made void of fear, or fright: or, accord. to IJ, fur~iga and fuz~iEa and A@foranoqaEa [which are all mentioned as readings in the same passage] have one meaning. (TA. [See 2 in art. fzE .]) ― -b2- [Hence one says, fr~ghu lika*aA He made him to be, or become, or he left him, vacant from, devoid of, or free from, business, occupation, or employment; or made him to be unoccupied, unemployed, or at leisure; so that he might apply himself exclusively to such a thing. ] ― -b3- See also the next paragraph.

definition: He was, or became, or he made himself to be, vacant from, devoid of, or free from, business, occupation, or employment;
sourceDefinition: He was, or became, or he made himself to be, vacant from, devoid of, or free from, business, occupation, or employment; unoccupied, unemployed, or at leisure; syn. taxal~aY mina Al$~ugoli . (O, K.) [See also faraga mina Al$~ugoli .] Hence the trad. of the Prophet, tafar~aguwA mino humuwmi Ald~unoyaA maA A@sotaTaEotumo [ Be ye, or make yourselves to be, vacant, or free, from the anxieties of the present state of existence as much as ye are able ]. (O.) ― -b2- And tafar~agotu lika*aA [ I was, or became, or I made myself to be, vacant, or free, from business, occupation, or employment; or unoccupied, unemployed, or at leisure; for such a thing: and I applied myself exclusively to such a thing ]: (S: [these meanings are there indicated, but not expressed; and are well known:]) one says, tfr~g liloEibaAdapi [ He applied himself exclusively to religious service ]: (Msb in art. btl :) and tafar~agotu liloA^amori means [also, simply,] taSad~ayotu lahu [i. e. I addressed, or applied, or directed, myself, or my regard, or attention, or mind, to the affair ]. (Msb in art. Sd .) [See also faraga lahu and A_ilayohi .] ― -b3- And tfr~g bihi signifies taxal~aY bihi [meaning He confined himself exclusively to it; or contented himself with it exclusively of other things ]. (K and TA in art. xlw .)

(TA.) ― -b3- Hence AlfarogaAni , (S, O,) farogu Ald~alowi Almuqad~amu and farogu Ald~alowi Almuw^ax~aru , (S, O, K,) or Alfarogu AlA^aw~alu and Alfarogu Alv~aAniY , (Kzw,) Two of the Mansions of the Moon, (S, O, K,) the Twenty-sixth Mansion and the Twentyseventh; four stars, wide apart, forming the corners of a square, or four-sided figure; (Kzw;) each consisting of two stars, (S, O, K, and Kzw,) of two bright stars, (S,) the apparent distance between each two stars being the measure of five cubits, (S, O, L,) or the measure of a spear; (K;) [see *iraAEN and rumoHN ; the former pair consists of the stars a and b of Pegasus; and the latter, of g in Pegasus together with the bright star in the head of Andromeda; as is shown by what here follows:] the Arabs name Ald~alowu the four bright stars in Pegasus which form a square, or four-sided figure; i. e., that at the extremity of the neck, which is called matonu Alfarasi , and that which is called manokibu Alfarasi , and that which is called janaAHu Alfarasi , and the star that belongs to both Pegasus and Andromeda: (Kzw, descr. of Pegasus:) [these two pairs of stars are what are commonly known as the farogaAni ; and are plainly indicated by the periods assigned to the auroral settings thereof: but the periods assigned to their auroral risings would lead us to apply the appel-lation of the frgAn to some other stars, not easily determinable, in Aquarius: see nawo'N : and see also manaAzilu Alqamari , in art. nzl .] The pl. Alfuruwgu is said to be applied to The farogaAni with the stars around them: (O, TA:) and (accord. to El-Jumahee, O, TA) Alfuruwgu [in the CK erroneously written Alfaruwgu ] signifies [ The constellation called ] AljawozaA='u . (O, K, TA. [But see furuwEu AljawozaA='i , in art. frE .]) ― -b4- farogN also signifies A vessel in which is [ the exuded, or expressed, juice termed ] dibos , (O, K,) and Saqor . (O.) ― -b5- Also Land affected with drought, or barrenness. (IB, TA.) ― -b6- See also the next paragraph.

(TA.) ― -b2- And fariygapN (tropical:) A mazaAdap [or leathern water-bag] that takes in much water; (O, K, TA;) as though having farog , i. e. width. (TA.) ― -b3- And friygN signifies also (tropical:) Land, or ground, that is even, or flat, as though it were a road, (O, K, TA,) and wide: (TA:) or that is marked by much treading: to such Aboo-Kebeer El-Hudhalee likens the whiteness of the A^avor , i. e. firinod , of a sword. (O, TA.) -A2- And (tropical:) A horse wide in step, (S, O, K, TA,) easy, or good, and quick, in pace; as also ↓ firaAgN : (O, K, TA:) or swift and excellent, wide in step: or quick in pace, wide in step, applied to a horse or the like; and so ↓ firaAgN , applied to an ass, and likewise to a man: and, accord. to Z, fariygN applied to an ass signifies wide in step. (TA.) ― -b2- Also Sharp, applied to an arrow, and likewise to a knife. (TA.) And (assumed tropical:) Sharp-tongued, applied to a man. (TA.)

definition: Empty, vacant, void, devoid, destitute, or unoccupied;
sourceDefinition: Empty, vacant, void, devoid, destitute, or unoccupied; syn. xaAlK ; as in the phrase A_inaA='N fArigN [ an empty vessel ]: (O, TA:) and likewise applied to a man, (O, TA, *) meaning vacant from, devoid of, or free from, business, occupation, or employment; (K, * TA;) as also ↓ farigN : (O, K, TA:) [and often, used elliptically, meaning vacant from, devoid of, or free from, business &c., and care or anxiety or disquietude; unoccupied, unemployed, or at leisure: ] and ↓ A^aforagu is syn. with faArigN ; (O, K;) as in the phrase, of Ru-beh, maA Alma$oguwlu mivolu AlA^aforagi [ The busied is not like the free from business ]: (O, TA:) [ fur~aAgN is pl. of faArigN : and] ↓ firogN is syn. with fur~aAgN ; (O, K; [in the former, as is often the case, the sign of tesh-deed in this word has been carelessly omitted; and in the CK, Alfragu is put for Alfur~aAgu , and has been erroneously supposed to be for AlfaraAgu ;]) for ex., Tuleyhah Ibn-Khuweylid El-Asadee says, in relation to the slaying of his brother's son, Hibál Ibn-Selemeh Ibn-Khuweylid, famaA Zan~ukumo biAlqawomi A_i*o taqotuluwnahumo A^alayosuwA waA_ino lamo yusolimuwA birijaAli faA_ino taku A^a*owaAdN A^uSibona wanisowapN falano ta*ohabuwA firogFA biqatoli HibaAli [ And what is your opinion of the party when ye slay them? Are they not ( though they have not become Muslims ) men? It is said in the Kur [xxviii. 9], waA^aSobaHa fw^aAdu A^um~i muwsaY faArigFA , meaning And the heart, or mind, of the mother of Moses became devoid of patience: or devoid of everything except remembering of Moses: or devoid of anxiety; because of God's having promised to restore him to her, (O, TA,) by words in the next but one of the preceding verses. (O.) [See also another reading voce firogN ; and another, voce furugN .] And it is said in a form of prayer, Aall~`hum~a A_in~iY A^asoA^aluka AlEayo$i Alr~aAfigi waAlmaAla AlfaAriga [ O God, I ask of Thee ample, or abundant, and pleasant, or good, means of subsistence, and cattle free from labour ]. (TA.) And one says, fulaAnN faArigN ma$oguwlN , meaning (assumed tropical:) Such a one is devoted to that which is unprofitable. (TA in art. $gl .) And h`*aA kalaAmN faArigN (tropical:) [ This is empty talk or language ]. (TA.)

definition: , (S, A, MA, Mgh, O, L, Msb, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, A, MA, Mgh, O, L, Msb, K,) aor. , (S, A, O, &c.,) inf. n. faqodN and fiqodaAnN (S, MA, O, L, Msb, K) and fuqodaAnN (S, O, F) and fuquwdN ; (IDrd, O, L, K;) and ↓ Aftqdhu ; (S, A, MA, Mgh, O;) He found it not, (L, TA,) lost it, (MA, PS, &c.,) saw it not, (JK in explanation of the latter verb,) [ missed, or failed of finding or seeing, it, ] it was, or became, absent from him, (Mgh,) or he had it not, was destitute of it, was without it, lacked it, or wanted it, syn. Eadimahu ; (Msb, L, K;) but accord. to Er-Rághib, Alfaqodu has a more special signification than AlEadamu , this latter being the contr. of Alwujuwdu ; (TA;) [whereas] Alfaqodu [as inf. n. of fuqida , though often used as meaning the being non-existent, properly] signifies the thing's being absent from the range of perception by sense so that its place is not known. (Bd in xii. 71.) [ fuqida signifies It was not found, was lost, was not seen, &c.] It is related of Abu-dDardà that he said, yafoqido ↓ mano yatafaq~ado , [lit. He who seeks will not find, ] meaning he who seeks after good in mankind will not find it; for he saw good to be rare in mankind: or he who seeks to acquaint himself with the circumstances of men will not find what will please him. (L.)

definition: He sought it, or sought for it or after it;
sourceDefinition: He sought it, or sought for it or after it; or did so leisurely or repeatedly; (A, * Mgh, L;) as also ↓ Aftqdhu : (Mgh, L:) or he sought it, or sought for it or after it, it being absent from him; (S, O, L, Msb, K;) as also ↓ Aftqdhu : (K:) or he sought, or sought leisurely or repeatedly, to obtain knowledge of it, having lost it: so accord. to Er-Rághib and many others; but this expression and tEah~adahu are used, by some, each in the place of the other, and the latter, accord. to Er-Rághib and many others, [properly] signifies he sought, or sought leisurely or repeatedly, to obtain knowledge of it, having known it before. sourceDefinition: Camels upon which the [ kind of saddle called ] qatab is bound: (S, A, O, K, TA:) or a camel upon which the qatab may be put: (Lh, TA:) the p is affixed because the word is similar to HaluwbapN and rakuwbapN , (S, O, TA,) having the signification of a pass. part. n.; but one may elide the p , saying ↓ qatuwbN . (A.)

(S.) ― -b2- And [hence] one says, qariHa qalobu Alr~ajuli mina AlHuzoni (assumed tropical:) [ The heart of the man became as though it were ulcerated by grief ]. (L.) ― -b3- qariHa , aor. , inf. n. qaraHN , said of a horse, He had a white mark in his face, such as is termed quroHap . (IAar, S.)

(Msb.) ― -b2- qur~iHa said of a camel: see 1, near the beginning. ― -b3- [ qr~Hhu biAlHaq~i in some copies of the K is a mistranscription; the verb in this phrase being without teshdeed.] ― -b4- qr~H Alwa$oma He pricked, or punctured, the w$m [or tattoo ] with the needle. (A.) ― -b5- And [the inf. n.] Alt~aqoriyHu signifies Alt~a$owiyku [by which may be meant The pricking with a thorn: or, as seems to be not improbable from what here follows, it may be from $w~k Alz~aroEu , q. v.]. (TA.) ― -b6- qr~H , (A,) inf. n. taqoriyHN , (TA,) said of the [plant called] Earofaj , means (tropical:) It put forth its first growth. (A, TA. *) And qr~H Al$~ajaru (tropical:) The trees put forth the heads [or extremities ] of their leaves. (A.) Accord. to AHn, Alt~aqoriyHu signifies (assumed tropical:) The first vegetation of herbs, or leguminous plants, that grow from grain, or seed: and the growing of the stalk of herbs, or leguminous plants; i. e. the appearing of the stem thereof: IAar uses the phrase yanobutu SulobFA ↓ Albaqolu muqotariHFA [as though meaning the herbs, or leguminous plants, grow putting forth the stem in a hard, or firm, state ]; but it should be ↓ muqar~iHFA , unless ↓ AiqotaraHa be a dial. var. of qar~aHa : or it may be that ↓ muqotariHFA here means standing upright upon the stem thereof. (TA.) taqoriyHu AlA^aroDi signifies The land's beginning to give growth to plants, or herbage. (TA.)

Hence one says, AqtrH Ealayohi Sawota ka*aA waka*aA (assumed tropical:) He desired of him in preference such and such an air, or such and such a tune or song. (IAar, L.) (Har ibid.) And AqtrH Ealayohi bika*aA (tropical:) He exercised his authority, or judgment, over him, in such a thing, and asked without consideration. (TA.) And AqtrH Ealayohi $ayoy^FA (tropical:) He asked of him a thing without consideration. (S, A.) -A2- See also 2, last sentence but one.

definition: and ↓ quroHN A wound;
sourceDefinition: and ↓ quroHN A wound; (L;) the bite of a weapon, and of a similar thing that wounds the body: (L, K: [but in some copies of the K, for EaD~u Als~ilaAHi wanaHowihi mim~aA yajoraHu Albadana (which is the reading in the CK), we find ED~ AlslAH wanaHowuhu mm~A yaxoruju biAlbadani , and the L and TA combine the two readings, the latter whereof gives a second signification, which will be found below:]) i. q. juroHN [with which jaroHN is held by many to be syn.]: (TA:) they are two dial. vars., (S, Msb,) like DaEofN and DuEofN , (S,) and jahodN and juhodN , (Fr, Msb, TA,) and wajodN and wujodN ; (Fr, TA;) the former of the dial. of El-Hijáz: (Msb:) or the former is an inf. n. and the latter is a simple subst.: (L, Msb:) or the former signifies as above; and the latter signifies its pain: (A:) or the latter seems to bear this latter signification; and the former, to signify wounds themselves: (Yaakoob, TA:) [and the like is said in the L and K:]) [and thus used in a pl. sense, the former is a coll. gen. n.;] and its n. un. is ↓ qaroHapN ; and pl. quruwHN : (L:) one says, bihi quroHN mino qaroHK In him is pain from a wound; (A;) or from wounds. (L.) ― -b2- qaroHN also signifies Pustules, or small swellings, when they have become corrupt; (L, K;) [i. e. purulent pustules; and imposthumes, ulcers, or sores: and so ↓ quroHN accord. to the L and some copies of the K, as shown above; but this seems to be of doubtful authority: qaroHN in this sense is a coll. gen. n.:] its n. un. is ↓ qaroHapN ; and pl. quruwHN . (S.) Imra-el-Keys (the poet, TA) was called *uw AlquruwHi because the King of the Greeks sent to him a poisoned shirt, from the wearing of which his body became affected with purulent pustules, or ulcers, or sores, ( taqar~aHa ,) and he died: (S, K, * TA:) or, as some say, he was called *uw AlfuruwjK , with f and j ; because he left only daughters. (Es-Suyootee, TA.) ― -b3- Also, (accord. to the K,) or ↓ quroHN , (as in the L,) A severe scab or mange, that destroys young weaned camels; (L, K;) or that attacks young weaned camels, and from which they scarcely ever, or never, recover: so says Lth: Az, however, says that this is a mistake; but that quroHapN signifies a certain disease that attacks camels, expl. below. (L.) -A2- See also qariyHN .

definition: A disease that attacks camels, consisting in quruwH [or purulent pustules ] in the mouth, in consequence of which the lip hangs down;
sourceDefinition: A disease that attacks camels, consisting in quruwH [or purulent pustules ] in the mouth, in consequence of which the lip hangs down; not scab, or mange. (Az, L, TA.) [See also qaroHN , near the end.] -A2- Also A gur~ap [meaning star, or blaze, or white mark, ] in the middle of the forehead of a horse: (T, L:) or what is less than a gur~ap in the face of a horse: (S, K:) or it is a whiteness in the forehead of a horse (Mgh) of the size of a dirhem, or smaller than it; (AO, Mgh, TA;) whereas the gur~ap is larger than a dirhem: (AO, TA:) or what is like a small dirhem between a horse's eyes: (En-Nadr, TA:) or any whiteness, in the face of a horse, which stops short of reaching the place of the halter upon the nose; differently distinguished in relation to its form, as being round, or triangular, or four-sided, or elongated, or scanty: (L, TA:) [and it is also applied to a white mark upon the face of the common fly: (see qaduwHN :) the pl. is quraHN , like gurarN .] ― -b2- [Hence] one says, huwa qaroHapu A^aSoHaAbihi i. e. gur~atuhumo [meaning (tropical:) He is the noble, or eminent, one of his companions; or the chief, or lord, of them ]. (A.) ― -b3- And [hence, likewise,] quroHapN signifies also (tropical:) The first, or commencement, of the [rain called] wasomiY~ ; (A;) and of the [season called] rabiyE ; or of the $itaA=' . (K.) ― -b4- See also quroHN .

definition: ([i. e. quroHaAnN or quroHaAnu ] with or without tenween, as you please, Sh, TA) A camel that has never been attached by the mange, or scab: (S, K:) and a child, (S, K,) or a man, (A,) that has never...
sourceDefinition: ([i. e. quroHaAnN or quroHaAnu ] with or without tenween, as you please, Sh, TA) A camel that has never been attached by the mange, or scab: (S, K:) and a child, (S, K,) or a man, (A,) that has never been attacked by the small-pox, (T, * S, A, K,) nor by the measles, (T, A,) nor by purulent pustules or the like: (T:) applied alike to one (S, K) and to two (S) and to a pl. number, (S, A, K,) and expl. as meaning persons not yet attacked by disease, (S,) and also applied alike to the male and to the female: (TA:) quroHaAnuwna [as a pl. thereof] is of weak authority, (K,) or disused. (S, A, L.) ― -b2- [Hence] one says, A^anota bihi ↓ quroHaAnN mim~aA quriHota i. e. (tropical:) Thou art clear [ of that whereof thou hast been accused ]. (A, TA.) And A^anota quroHaAnN mino h`*aA AlA^amori (tropical:) Thou art quit of this affair; and so ↓ quraAHiY~N . (Az, K, TA.) ― -b3- And quroHaAn signifies also One who has not witnessed war; and so ↓ quraAHiY~N : ― -b4- and One who has been touched by quruwH [here app. meaning wounds, and perhaps also purulent pustules ]: thus having contr. significations: (K:) masc. and fem. definition: , (S, A, Mgh, O, Msb, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, A, Mgh, O, Msb, K,) aor. , (Msb, K.) inf. n. qalobN , (Msb,) He altered, or changed, its, or his, mode, or manner, of being; (A, Mgh, Msb, * K;) and ↓ ql~bhu signifies the same, (K,) or is like qalabahu in the sense expl. above and in other senses but denotes intensiveness and muchness; (Msb;) and ↓ Aqlbhu also signifies the same as qalabahu in the sense expl. above, (K,) on the authority of Lh, but is of weak authority. (TA.) Hence, (Mgh,) He inverted it; turned it upside-down; turned it so as to make its upper most part its undermost; (S, * A, * Mgh, Msb;) namely, a thing; (S;) for instance, a [garment of the kind called] ridaA=' : (A, * Mgh:) and ↓ ql~bhu has a similar meaning, but [properly] denotes intensiveness and muchness. (Msb. See two exs. of the latter verb voce qalabapN .) And, (A, K,) like ↓ ql~bhu , [except that the latter properly denotes intensiveness and muchness,] (K,) it signifies Haw~alahu ZahorFA libaTonK (A, K) [ He turned it over, or upsidedown as meaning so that the upper side became the under side; lit. back for belly; accord. to the TA, meaning back upon belly ( ZahorFA EalaY baTonK ); but this is hardly conceivable; whereas the former explanation is obviously right in another case: (see 5:) and another meaning of qalabahu and ↓ qulbhu , i. e. he turned it inside-out, is indicated in the TA by its being added, so that he knew what was in it ]. ― -b2- See an ex. voce qalaAbi . One says, qalaba kalaAmFA [meaning He altered, or changed, the order of the words of a sentence or the like, by inversion, or by any transposition ]. (TA.) [And in like manner, qalaba kalimapF He altered, or changed, the order of the letters of a word, by inversion, or by any transposition. ] Es-Sakháwee says, in the Expos. of the Mufassal, that when they transpose [the letters of a word], they do not assign to the [transformed] derivative an inf. n., lest it should be confounded with the original, using only the inf. n. of the original that it may be an evidence of the originality [of the application of the latter to denote the signification common to both]: thus they say yay^isa , inf. n. yaA^osN ; and A^ayisa is minohu ↓ maqoluwbN [i. e. formed by transposition, or metathesis, from it ], and has no inf. n.: when the two inf. ns. exist, the grammarians decide that each of the two verbs is [to be regarded as] an original, and that neither is mqlwb from the other, as in the case of ja*aba and jaba*a : but the lexicologists [in general] assert that all such are [of the class termed] mqlwb . (Mz, close of the 33rd nwE .) [And qalaba likewise signifies He changed, or converted, a letter into another letter; the verb in this sense being doubly trans.: for ex., one says, qalaba AlwaAwa yaA='F He changed, or converted, the w into Y .] ― -b3- And [hence] one says, qalabahu Eano wajohihi (assumed tropical:) He turned him [ from his manner, way, or course, of acting, or proceeding, &c.]: and Lh has mentioned ↓ Aqlbhu [in the same sense], but as being disapproved. (TA.) And qalaba AlS~iboyaAna (tropical:) He (the teacher) turned away [or dismissed ] the boys to their dwellings: (Th, A, TA:) or sent them [ away ], and returned them, to their abodes: and Lh has mentioned ↓ Aqlbhm as a dial. var. of weak authority, saying that the former verb is that which is used by the Arabs in this and other [similar] cases. sourceDefinition: [ The thing turned over and over, or upside-down as meaning so that the upper side became the under side, (lit. back for belly, ) doing so much, or repeatedly ], like as does the serpent upon the ground vehemently heated by the sun. (S, O, TA.) tql~b said of a man's face [&c.] signifies tSr~f [i. e. It turned about, properly meaning much, or in various ways or directions; or it was, or became, turned about, &c.]. (Jel in ii. 139.) And tataqal~abu fiyhi A@loquluwbu waA@loA^aboSaAru , in the Kur [xxiv. 37], means In which the hearts and the eyes shall be in a state of commotion, or agitation, by reason of fear, (Zj, Jel, TA,) and impatience; (Zj, TA;) the hearts between safety and perdition, and the eyes between the right side and the left. (Jel.) And fiY taqal~ubihimo , in the Kur xvi. 48, means (assumed tropical:) In their journeyings for traffic. (Jel. [See also the Kur iii. 196, and xl. 4.]) You say, tql~b fiY AlbilaAdi , (TA,) and fY AlA^umuwri , (K, TA,) meaning taSar~afa fiyhaA kayofa $aA='a [i. e. (assumed tropical:) He acted in whatsoever way he pleased, according to his own judgment or discretion or free will, or as a free agent, in journeying, for traffic or otherwise, in the country, and in the disposal, or management, of affairs: and simply, he employed himself in journeying, for traffic or otherwise, in the country, and in the disposal, or management, of affairs: or tql~b fY AlAmwr means he practised versatility, or used art or artifice or cunning, in the disposal, or management, of affairs ]. (K, * TA.) sourceDefinition: The heart; syn. fuw^aAdN : (Lh, T, S, M, O, Msb, K, &c.:) or [accord. to some] it has a more special signification than the latter word: (O, K:) [for] some say that fw^Ad signifies the “ appendages of the mariYo' [or œsophagus], consisting of the liver and lungs and qalob [or heart]: ” (K in art. fA^d :) [and, agreeably with this assertion,] it is said that the qlb is a lump of flesh, pertaining to the fw^Ad , suspended to the niyaAT [q. v.]: Az says, I have observed that some of the Arabs call the whole flesh of the qlb , its fat, and its HijaAb [or septum?], qalob and fuw^aAd ; and I have not observed them to distinguish between the two [words]; but I do not deny that the [word] qlb may be [applied by some to] the black clot of blood in its interior: MF mentions that fw^Ad is said to signify the “ receptacle, ” or “ covering, ” of the heart, ( wiEaA='u Alqalobi , or gi$aAw^uhu , [i. e. the pericardium,]) or, accord. to some, its “ interior: ” the qalob is said to be so called from its taqal~ub : [see 5:] the word is of the masc. gender: and the pl. is quluwbN . (TA.) banaAtu Alqalobi means (assumed tropical:) The several parts, or portions, [or, perhaps, appertenances, ] of the heart. (TA in art. bnY .) [And qalobN is also used as meaning The stomach, which is often thus termed in the present day: so, for ex., in an explanation of Tanix , q. v.] ― -b2- qalobu AlEaqorabi (also called simply, Alqalobu , Kzw) is (assumed tropical:) A certain bright star, [ the star a in Scorpio, ] between two other stars, which is one of the Mansions of the Moon, (S, O,) namely, the Eighteenth Mansion; so called because it is in the heart of Scorpio: (MF:) [it rose aurorally, about the commencement of the era of the Flight, in Central Arabia, together with Aln~asoru AlwaqiEu (a of Libra) on the 25th of November, O. S.: (see manaAzilu Alqamari , in art. nzl :)] the commencement of the period when the cattle breed in the desert is at the time of its [auroral] rising and the [auroral] rising of Alnsr AlwAqE ; these two stars rising together, in the cold season: the Arabs say, Alqalbo jaA='a Al$~itaA='u kaA@lokalobo [ When the heart of the Scorpion rises, the winter comes like the dog ]: and they regard its nawo' [q. v.] as unlucky; and dislike journeying when the moon is in Scorpio: at its nawo' [meaning auroral rising], the cold becomes vehement, cold winds blow, and the sap becomes stagnant in the trees: its raqiyb is Ald~abaraAnu [q. v.] (Kzw.) There are also three similar appellations of other stars: these are qalobu AlA^asadi (assumed tropical:) [ Cor Leonis, or Regulus, the star a of Leo ]: qalobu Alv~awori , an [improper] appellation of Ald~abaraAnu : and qalobu AlHuwti , a name of Alr~i$aA='u [q. v.]. (TA.) ― -b3- And Alqalobu is syn. with AlD~amiyru [signifying (assumed tropical:) The heart as meaning the mind or the secret thoughts ]. (Msb in art. Dmr .) ― -b4- And (assumed tropical:) The soul. (TA.) ― -b5- And (assumed tropical:) The mind, meaning the intellect, or intelligence. (Fr, S, O, Msb, K.) So in the Kur l. 36: (Fr, S, O, TA:) or it means there endeavour to understand, and consideration. (TA.) Accord. to Fr, you may say, maA laka qalobN (assumed tropical:) Thou hast no intellect, or intelligence: (TA:) and maA qalobuka maEaka (assumed tropical:) Thine intellect is not present with thee: (O, TA:) and A^ayona *ahaba qalobuka (assumed tropical:) Whither has thine intellect gone? (TA.) [And hence, A^afoEaAlu Alquluwbi (assumed tropical:) The verbs significant of operations of the mind; as Zan~a , and the like.] ― -b6- See also qulobN . ― -b7- [ qalobu Aljayo$i means (assumed tropical:) The main body of the army; as distinguished from the van and the rear and the two wings: mentioned in the S and K in art. xms ; &c.] ― -b8- And qalobN signifies also (assumed tropical:) The pure, or choice, or best, part of anything. (L, K, * TA.) It is said in a trad. A_in~a likul~i $aYo'K qalobFA waqalobu AlquroA=ni y`s= (tropical:) [as though meaning, Verily to everything there is a choice, or best, part; and the choice, or best, part of the Kur-án is Yá-Seen (the Thirty-sixth Chapter)]: (A, O, L, TA:) it is a saying of the Prophet; [and may (perhaps better) be rendered, verily to everything there is a pith; and the pith &c.; from qalobN , as meaning, like qulobN , the “ pith ” of the palm-tree; but,] accord. to Lth, it is from what here immediately follows. (O.) One says, jiy^otuka bih`*aA AlA^amori qalobFA , meaning (tropical:) I have come to thee with this affair unmixed with any other thing. (A, * O, L, TA.) ― -b9- Also (tropical:) A man genuine, or pure, in respect of origin, or lineage; (S, A, O, K;) holding a middle place among his people; (A;) and ↓ qulobN signifies the same: (O, K:) the former is used alike as masc. and fem. and sing. and dual and pl.; but it is allowable to form the fem. and dual and pl. from it: (S, O:) one says EarabiY~N qalobN (S, A, * O) and ↓ qulobN (O) (tropical:) a genuine Arabian man, (S, A, * O,) and AimoraA^apN qalobN (S, * A, O *) and qalobapN (S, A, O) and ↓ qulobapN (K) a woman genuine, or pure, in respect of origin, or lineage: (S, A, * O, K:) Sb says, they said h`*aA EarabiY~N qalobN and qalobFA (assumed tropical:) [ This is an Arabian genuine, or pure, &c., and being genuine, or pure, &c.]; using the same word as an epithet and as an inf. n.: and it is said in a trad., kaAna EalY~N qura$iy~FA qalobFA , meaning (assumed tropical:) 'Alee was a Kurashee genuine, or pure, in respect of race: or, as some say, the meaning is, an intelligent manager of affairs; from qalobN as used in the Kur l. 36. (L, TA.)

sourceDefinition: (S, A, Mgh, O, Msb, K) and ↓ qalobN (S, O, Msb, K) and ↓ qilobN (S, O, K) (tropical:) The lub~ , (S, O,) or $aHomap , (A, K,) or jum~aAr , (Mgh, Msb,) [i. e. heart, or pith, ] of the palm-tree; (S, A, Mgh, O, Msb, K;) which is a soft, white substance, that is eaten; it is in the midst of its uppermost part, and of a pleasant, or sweet, taste: (TA: [see also jum~aArN :]) or the best of the leaves of the palm-tree, (AHn, K [in which this explanation relates to all the three forms of the word, but app. accord. to AHn it relates only to the first of them], and TA,) and the whitest; which are the leaves next to the uppermost part thereof; and one of these is termed ↓ qulobapN , with damm and sukoon: (AHn, TA:) or qulobN , with damm, signifies the branches of the palm-tree ( saEaf [in my copy of the Msb sEfp ]) that grow forth from the qlb [meaning heart ]: (T, TA: [see AlEawaAhinu and AlxawaAfiY , pls. of EaAhinN , or EaAhinapN , and xaAfiyapN :]) the pl. is qilabapN , (S, O, Msb, K,) which is of the second, (Msb,) [or of all,] and quluwbN , (Msb, K,) a pl. of the second, (Msb,) and A^aqolaAbN , (Msb, K,) a pl. [of pauc.] of the first. (Msb.) ― -b2- And qulobN signifies also (tropical:) A bracelet (S, O, K, TA) that is worn by a woman, (K, TA,) such as is one qulob , (S, O, TA, but in the O, one qalob ,) [as though meaning such as is single, not double, ] or such as is one qilod , ('Eyn, T, MS, [and this is evidently the right reading, as will be shown by what follows,]) meaning such as is formed by twisting [or rather bending round ] one TaAq [i. e. one wire (more or less thick), likened to a yarn, or strand], not of a double TaAq ; (MS;) and they say siwaArN qulobN ; (TA;) and qulobu fiD~apK i. e. a [woman's] bracelet [ of silver ], (A, Mgh, Msb, TA,) such as is not twisted [like a cord, or rope, of two or more strands, as are many of the bracelets worn by Arab women]: (Mgh, Msb, TA:) so called as being likened to the qulob of the palm-tree because of its whiteness; (A, Mgh, Msb, TA;) or, as some say, the converse is the case. (Mgh.) ― -b3- And (tropical:) A serpent: (S, O:) or a white serpent: (A, K:) likened to the bracelet so called. sourceDefinition: There is not in him any disease, (S, A, Mgh,) thus says IAar, adding, for which he should be turned over (↓ yuqal~ab ) and examined, (S,) and in this sense it is said of a camel [and the like], (TA,) or on account of which he should turn over upon his bed: (A:) or there is not in him anything to disquiet him, so that he should turn over upon his bed: (Et-Tá-ee, TA:) or thers is not in him any disease, and any fatigue, (K, TA,) and any pain: (TA:) or there is not in him anything; said of one who is sick; and the word is not used otherwise than in negative phrases: accord. to IAar, originally used in relation to a horse or the like, meaning there is not in him any disease for which his hoof should be turned upsidedown (↓ yuqal~ab ) [ to be examined ]: (TA:) or it is from AlqulaAbu , (Fr, S, A, TA,) the disease, so termed, that attacks camels; (TA;) or from quliba [q. v.] as said of a man, and means there is not in him any disease on account of which one should fear for him. (S, TA.)

definition: [ Brimstone, or sulphur;
sourceDefinition: [ Brimstone, or sulphur; ] a thing well known; (S, art. kbr ;) one of the kinds of stone with which fire is kindled, or it (red kbryt TA) is a mineral whereof the mine is beyond EtTubbat, [ or the country of Et-Tibbet, in Tartary, ] in the Valley of the Ants, (K,) by which Solomon passed, (TA,) [as related in the Kur, xxvii. 18]: or [the product of ] a spring, or source, whereof the water, when it congeals, becomes white, and yellow, and dusky-coloured, kbryt : (Lth, in the T:) MF says, I have seen it in several places; among these, in one which is near El-Maláleeh, between Fás and Miknáseh; by swimming in which, persons are cured of the venereal disease, and other disorders: also in Africa Proper, in the midst of Barkah, in a place called Albrj ; and in other places: (TA:) Aristotle says, that, among the different kinds of kbryt are the red, of an excellent colour; and the white, which resembles dust; and the yellow: the source of the red is in the West: it does not appear in its place: the yellow is found near the ocean, a league (or leagues, as in the TA,) from it: it is useful in cases of epilepsy, and apoplexy, and megrim, and palpitation: and it enters into the preparations of gold: the white blackens white substances; and it is sometimes mixed and concealed in the sources of running water, which sources have a fetid odour: the person who plunges into these waters in times when the air is temperate is cured by them of wounds, and swellings, and scab, and wind in the womb, and [ the leprosy called ] salaE , that arises from black bile: Ibn-Seenà [Avicenna] also says, that kbryt , untouched by fire, is one of the remedies for the leprosy ( baraS ): that, mixed with the gum of the turpentine-tree, it removes marks on the nails: that, mixed with vinegar, it removes the [ leprous-like discolouration of the skin called ] bahaq , and the ringworm, or tetter, ( quwabaA' ,) especially with the gum of the turpentine-tree: that, with natron and water, it is an embrocation for the baraS [or, as in the TA, for the niqoris , or gout ): and that fumigation therewith stops a rheum: and others say, that, if yellow kbryt be powdered, and sprinkled upon a place affected with slEp , it has a good effect: that fumigation therewith whitens the hair: that serpents and fleas flee from the scent of it, especially if [ mixed ] with an unguent, or with the hoof of an ass; and that the fumigation therewith beneath a citrontree of the kind called A^utoruj~ causes all the fruits of it to fall. (El-Kazweenee.) Several authors say, that the t in kbryt is an augmentative letter, and that the proper place of the word is in art. kbr . IDrd thinks it to be not genuine Arabic. (TA.) [Golius thinks it to be from the Persian kuwkurodo (or kuwkurodo ): or rather, he adds, from the Hebrew נּפְּרִיח Gen. xix. 24.] ― -b2- A^aEaz~umina Alkiboriyti AlA^aHomari [ More rare than red brimstone, or sulphur ]. A proverb. Some say, that kbryt AHmr [meaning as above] is a thing that does not exist: others, that by it is meant gold. (Meyd.) This phrase is similar to A^aEaz~u mino bayoDi AlA^anuwqi . (S, art. kbr .) ― -b3- kiboriytN also signifies gold: (K:) [see above:] or red gold: or red [as an epithet applied to gold]: (TA:) or pure, as an epithet applied to gold. (S, art. kbr .) Ru-beh says, halo yanofaEan~iY ka*ibN sixotiytu A^awo fiD~apN A^awo *ahabN kiboriytu [ Will vehement lying profit me, or silver, or pure gold? ] (S, art. kbr .) IAar says, Ru-beh imagined that kbryt meant gold: upon which MF observes, that the ancient Arabs erred with respect to meanings, though not with respect to words. The latter author, however, supposes kbryt to be fig. used as signifying gold; for they use the expression Alkbryt AlAHmr [as applied to gold] because gold is [said to be] prepared therefrom, and it is used in alchymical processes. (TA.) ― -b4- kiboriytN also signifies The red jacinth, or ruby; syn. yaAquwtN A^aHomaru . (K.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. ka*ibN (a strange form of inf. n.; there being, accord. to Kz., only fourteen instances of it; as laEibN , and DaHikN , &c.; though there are many substantives of this measure; MF) and ki*obN (S, K: accord. to Ibn-Es-Seed and others, this latter is formed from the former, by putting the second vowel of the former in the place of the first: MF) and ka*ibapN (L) or ka*obapN (K) and ki*obahN (L, K) and ki*aAbN and ki*~aAbN (K: but this last, which is also assigned to ka*aba in the L, is, accord. to the S, which refers, for proof, to the Kur, ch. lxxviii. 28, one of the inf. ns. of k*~b : and Ks says, that the people of El-Yemen make the inf. n. of fE~l of the measure fiE~aAlN , while the other Arabs make it tafoEiylN : TA) and, accord. to some, ku*obN and ka*obN (TA: but the latter of these two, though agreeable with analogy, is unheard: TA): see also ka*ibN , below: [ He lied; uttered a falsehood; said what was untrue: ] he gave an untrue account, or relation, of a thing, whether intentionally or unintentionally. (Msb) Alka*ibu is of five kinds. ― -b2- First, The relater's changing, or altering, what he hears; and his relating; as from others, what he does not know. This is the kind that renders one criminal, and destroys manly virtue. — Second, The saying what resembles a lie, not meaning anything but the truth. Such is meant in the trad., ka*aba A_ibor`hiymu valaAva ka*ibaAtK Abraham said three sayings resembling lies; he being veracious in the three. — Third, The saying what is untrue by mistake, or unintentionally; making a mistake; erring. This signification is frequent. — Fourth, The finding one's hopes false, or vain. — Fifth, The act of instigating, or inciting. (IAmb.) [See illustrations of these and other significations below; and see more voce Sadaqa .] [You say] yako*ibuka mino A^ayona jaA'a [ He will lie to thee even as to the place whence he comes. ] (L, art. mH , and in many other places, following the similar phrase laA yaSoduquka A^avarahu , or A^avaruhu .) Lebeed says, Aiko*ibi Aln~afosa A_i*aA Had~avotahaA Lie to the soul (i. e., to thy soul, ) when thou talkest to it: i. e., say not to thy soul, Thou wilt not succeed in thine enterprise; for thy doing so will divert thee, or hinder thee, therefrom. A proverb. (Meyd, &c.) ― -b3- ku*iba , pass., He was told a lie; a falsehood; or an untruth. (K.) ― -b4- Aboo-Duwád says, ka*aba AlEayoru waA_ino kaAna baraHo The wild ass hath lied, although he hath passed from right to left: [the doing which is esteemed unlucky:] or, [agreeably with explanations of ka*aba given below,] hath become languid, and within [ the sportsman's ] power, or reach, &c.: or keep to the wild ass, and hunt him, &c. A proverb, applied in the case of a thing that is hoped for, though difficult of attainment. (TA.) ― -b5- ka*abato and ↓ k*~bt (tropical:) She (a camel), being covered by the stallion, raised her tail, and then returned without conceiving. (En-Nadr, K.) ― -b6- ka*aba is said of other things than men [and animals]: as of lightning, [meaning (assumed tropical:) It gave a false promise of rain ]: of a dream, an opinion, a hope, and a desire, [meaning, in each of these cases, (assumed tropical:) It proved false ]. (TA.) ― -b7- So also ka*abati AlEayonu (assumed tropical:) The sense [i. e., the sight ] of the eye deceived it. (TA.) ― -b8- ka*aba Alr~aA^oYu [(assumed tropical:) The judgment lied ]; i. e., he imagined the thing contrary to its real state. (TA.) [See also Sadaqa Zan~iY ] ― -b9- ka*abatoka Eayonuka (tropical:) Thine eye showed thee what had no reality. (TA.) ― -b10- ka*aba labanu Aln~aAqapi , and ↓ k*~b , (the latter mentioned in the S,) (tropical:) The milk of the camel passed away, or failed. (Lh.) ― -b11- ka*aba fiY sayorihi (tropical:) [ He (a camel) became slack, or slow, in his pace: see 2]. (TA.) ― -b12- ka*aba AlHar~u (tropical:) The heat abated. (TA.) ― -b13- See also 2. ka*aba He found his hopes to be false, or vain. (IAmb.) AunoZuro kayofa ka*abuwA EalaY A^anofusihimo , [Kur vi. 24, lit., See how they lied against themselves, ] is said to signify see how their hope hath proved false, or vain. (TA.) ― -b14- Zan~uwA A^an~ahumo qado ku*ibuwA , [Kur xii. 110,] They (the apostles) thought that they had been disappointed of the fulfilment of the promise made to them. So accord. to one reading. Accord. to another reading, the verb is ↓ ku*~ibuwA : [in which case, the meaning of the words appears to be, “ They knew that they had been pronounced liars ” by the people to whom they were sent]. (TA.) There are also two other readings; ↓ ka*~abuwA and ka*abuwA : accord. to the former, the verb refers to the people to whom the apostles were sent; and Zn~wA means “ they knew: ” accord. to the latter, the words mean, “ They (the people above mentioned) thought that they (the apostles) had broken their promise. ” (Jel.) ― -b15- maA ka*aba Alfuw^aAdu maA raA^aY [ The mind did not belie what he saw. ] (Kur liii. 11.) ― -b16- ka*abatohu nafosuhu [ His soul lied to him: ] his soul made him to desire things, and to conceive hopes, that could scarcely come to pass. (K.) Hence the soul is called Alka*uwbu . You say in the contr. case, Sa*aqatohu nfsh , and Alka*uwbu . (TA.) See ka*uwbN , and art. Sdq . ― -b17- Hence, ka*aba Ealayohi signifies It rendered him active, or brisk; animated him; instigated him; incited him; (K;) as also ka*abahu . (Z.) ― -b18- Hence, ka*aba and ka*abaka and ka*aba Ealayoka have sometimes the same signification, though not always the same government, as Ealayoka , or Ailozamo ; Keep to; or take to. The noun following is put in the nom. case accord. to the dial. of El-Yemen; and in the acc. accord. to the dial. of Mudar; or, as some say, is correctly put in the nom. only. (TA.) You say, ka*aba Ealayoka ka*aA waka*aA , meaning Keep to, or take to, such and such things. It is an extr. phrase. (ISk.) You also say, ka*abotu Ealayoka , meaning Keep thou to me: and k*btu Ealayokumo Keep ye to me. IAar. cites the following verse of Khidásh Ibn-Zuheyr, [in which he tauntingly compares a people to ticks]: ka*abotu Ealayokumo A^awo EiduwniY waEal~iluwA biYa AlA^aroDa waAlA^aqowaAma qirodaAna mawoZabaA [ Keep ye to me: threaten me, and soothe by ( the mention of ) me the land and the peoples, O ticks of Mowdhab! ]: meaning Keep ye to me, and to satirizing me, when ye are on a journey, and traverse the land mentioning me. (TA.) In like manner, yawomu AlA^aHadi wAlxamiysi ka*abaAka A^awo yawomu AlA_ivonayoni wAlv~alaAvaA'i , in a trad. respecting the proper days for being cupped, signifies Keep thou to Sunday and Thursday, or Monday and Tuesday. (IAth, Z.) The verb is thus used after the manner of a proverb, and is invariable [as to tense], being constantly in the pret. tense, connected [literally or virtually, when explained by Ealayoka followed by the prep. b , or by A_ilozamo ,] only with the person addressed, and in the sense of the imperative. k*bAk here [lit.] signifies Let them render thee active, or brisk, and animate thee, instigate thee, or incite thee. (Z.). [A trad. of 'Omar, quoted below, presents another instance to which this signification is said to apply.] ― -b19- Or ka*aba denotes instigation, or incitement, of the person addressed, to keep to the thing that is mentioned; as in the saying of the Arabs, ka*aba Ealayoka AlEasalu , meaning Eat thou honey: but the explanation of this is, ( The relinquisher of ) honey hath erred [ to thee; i. e., in his representation of its evil qualites &c.; which is equivalent to saying, Eat, or keep to, honey ]: AlEasalu being put for taAriku AlEasali . [See also 1 in art. Esl .] In like manner, the saying of 'Omar, ka*aba Ealayokumu AlHaj~u &c., (see below,) signifies Keep ye to the performance of the pilgrimage, &c.: [or ( the relinquisher of ) the pilgrimage hath erred to thee in his representation of it: therefore it means as above]. (IAmb.) Accord. to IAmb the noun signifying the object of instigation [which may also be called the cause thereof] cannot be rightly put in the acc. case: if so put, the verb is without an agent. (TA.) [But see what is said on this point in the remarks on the trad. of 'Omar below.] ― -b20- Or the verb in a case of this kind signifies A^amokana : thus, ka*abaka AlHaj~u signifies The performance of the pilgrimage is possible, or practicable, to thee: therefore [it means] Perform thou the pilgrimage. (ISh.) ― -b21- Or A^amokana is its original signification; and the meaning intended is Keep to; as in the ex. ka*aba AlEatiyqu . (Aal.) ― -b22- 'Antarah, addressing his wife 'Ableh, says; or, accord. to some, the poet is Khuzaz Ibn-Lowdhán; ka*aba AlEatiyqu wamaA='u $an~K baAridN A_ino kunoti saAy^ilatiY gabuwqFA faA@*ohabiY (TA.) i. e., Keep thou to the eating of dates, and to the cool water of an old, worn-out, skin: if thou ask me for an evening's drink of milk, depart: for I have appropriated the milk to my colt, which is profitable to me, and may preserve me and thee: (L:) AlEtyq is in the nom. case accord. to the dial. of El-Yemen: but in the acc. accord. to that of Mudar. (TA.) ― -b23- Er-Radee [reading AlEtyqa ] cites this verse as a proof that ka*aba , originally a verb, has become a verbal noun, signifying Ailozamo . (TA.) But he is the only one who asserts it to be a verbal noun. (MF.) ― -b24- Also, Mo'akkir El-Bárikee says, wa*uboyaAniy~apK A^uwoSato baniyhaA biA^ano ka*aba AlqaraATifu waAlquruwfu And many a woman of Dhubyán charged her sons by [ saying ], Keep to the red garments ( Aksyp ), and the bags (or receptacles ) of leather tanned with pomegranate-bark. She charged them to take plenty of these two things as spoil from the tribe of Nemir, if they should prevail over them. (Aboo-'Obeyd El-Kásim Ibn-Selám.) ― -b25- k*b is also said to have the same meaning in the words of the trad. ka*aba Aln~as~aAbuwna [ Keep to those skilled in genealogy: ] or Regard is to be had to what is said by those skilled in genealogy: another meaning to which is assigned below. (TA.) ― -b26- It sometimes signifies It is incumbent, or obligatory. So in the following: (a trad. of 'Omar: TA:) ka*aba Ealayokumu AlHaj~u ka*aba Ealayokumu AlEumorapu ka*aba Ealayokumu AljihaAdu vlaAvapu A^asofaArK ka*abona Ealayokumo [ The performance of the pilgrimage is incumbent on you: the performance of ( the rites called ) AlEmrp is incumbent on you: warring ( for the sake of religion ) is incumbent on you: three expeditions are incumbent on you ]: (S, * K:) or k*b , here, is from ka*abatohu nafosuhu , “ his soul made him to desire things, and to conceive hopes, that could scarcely come to pass; ” and the meaning is let [ the expectation of the reward which will follow ] the performance of the pilgrimage render thee active, or brisk, and animate thee, instigate thee, or incite thee, to the act: [and so of the rest of the trad.: but here I should observe, that, for liyako*ibaka and liyuna$~iTaka and yaboEavaka , in the CK, we should read liyako*iboka &c.:] (K:) ― -b27- or, as ISk says, k*b , here, seems to denote instigation, or incitement, meaning Ealayokumo bihi keep ye to it; and is an extr. word with respect to analogy: (S:) ― -b28- accord. to Akh., AlHj~ is governed in the nom. case by k*b ; but as to the meaning, it is in the acc.; because the meaning is a command to perform the pilgrimage; as when you say, A^amokanaka AlS~ayodu [“ the game hath become within thy power, or reach ”], meaning “ shoot it, ” or “ cast at it: ” (S:) he who puts AlHj~ in the acc. case, [agreeably with one relation of the trad., TA,] makes Elyk [or Elykm ] a verbal noun; and in k*b is [implied] the pronoun which refers to AlHj~ [and which is the agent of the verb]; (K;) or the agent is implied in k*b , and explained by what follows it; (Sb;) [so that] the meaning is ka*aba AlHaj~u Ealayokumu AlHaj~a : (Z:) or, [as shown above,] k*b is a verbal n., meaning Alozamo , and AlHj~ is in the acc. case as governed by it: (Er-Radee:) though its being in the acc. case, accord. to some, is altogether unknown: (TA:) ― -b29- [or the meaning is as stated before on the authority of ISh.:] ― -b30- or the trad. means ka*aba Ealayoka AlHaj~u A_ino *ukira A^an~ahu gayoru kaAfK haAdimK limaA qabolahu mina Al*~unuwbi [( the relinguisher of ) the pilgrimage hath erred to thee if it have been spoken of (by him) as not sufficient, (and as not) abolishing the sins, or offences, (committed) before it: agreeably with the explanation by IAmb, given above]. (K.) ― -b31- ka*aba He said what was false unintentionally; committed a mistake, or error. The verb is used in this sense by the people of El-Hijáz, and the rest of the Arabs have followed them in so using it. (Towsheeh.) -A2- ka*aba is also said to signify He spoke truth; so as to bear two contr. meanings: and thus, ka*aba Aln~as~aAbuwna may signify Those skilled in genealogy have spoken truth: but another explanation of this saying is given in this art. (MF, &c.) -A3- ka*abato Eaf~aAqatuka [and the like] Thou brokest wind. (S in art. Efq .)
